explanation: The hypothesis addresses oxidation resistance and scale integrity in high-temperature multiprincipal-element alloys and proposes a controlled, falsifiable dopant series with useful kinetic, microstructural, and adhesion measurements. The cited evidence directly supports Y segregation, interfacial Y2O3 particles, scale pinning, and improved adhesion, although it does not establish that progressively increasing Y in the proposed FeNiCuAl alloy will produce a monotonic benefit. It is not a reconstruction of the target study: it changes the alloy, intervention, baseline, and exposure mode from aging-induced L12/L21 precipitation followed by isothermal oxidation to Y addition and thermal cycling. It consequently misses the target mechanism in which Cr depletion and precipitate interfaces delay formation of a continuous Cr2O3 barrier, as well as the observed higher mass gain of the aged state. The boundary is only broadly stated and does not address exposure duration, dopant solubility or an optimum concentration window. E1 is labeled conflicting even though it supports the general reactive-element mechanism and merely excludes reactive-element concentration as the cause of a different comparison. Overall, this is a scientifically plausible but established reactive-element-effect alternative rather than the hidden precipitation/Cr-transport hypothesis.
